data.title: Šarišské Sokolovce – a Slavic hillfort on the Lazíky ridge
data.excerpt: Three kilometres north of Šarišské Sokolovce, on the highest point of the Lazíky ridge in the Čergov Mountains, lies a classic example of a Slavic hillfort in eastern Slovakia. J. Macák was alerted to it by the folk name of the hill, by its ramparts and ditches and by a dark occupation layer laid bare by a tractor, and V. Budinský-Krička trenched the site in 1965. The cuts revealed ramparts of differing construction and date, Hillfort-period pottery, iron weapons and slag from a smithy.
data.metaTitle: Šarišské Sokolovce – a Slavic hillfort in Čergov
data.metaDescription: A Slavic hillfort on the Lazíky ridge in the Čergov Mountains, excavated from 1965 by V. Budinský-Krička after its discovery by J. Macák.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: 3 km north of Šarišské Sokolovce, on the highest point of the Lazíky ridge in the Čergov Mountains

keyFacts.label: Dimensions
keyFacts.value: Greatest length of the hillfort 253 m, greatest width 125 m

keyFacts.label: System of ramparts
keyFacts.value: Several ramparts of differing construction and date — the acropolis rampart (timber construction, 9th century), a circuit rampart, a rampart dividing the bailey, ditches

keyFacts.label: Discovered by
keyFacts.value: J. Macák, on the basis of the folk name of the hill, the ramparts and ditches, and a dark occupation layer laid bare by a tractor

keyFacts.label: Smithing
keyFacts.value: Pieces of iron slag (iron oxides worked at over 1,200 °C) attest smithing, not iron smelting, at the hillfort

keyFacts.label: Finds
keyFacts.value: A fire-steel, a small knife, three arrowheads with backward barbs, a leaf-shaped spearhead (9th century), Hillfort-period pottery, a pre-Slavic sherd of the Late Bronze Age

keyFacts.label: Excavators
keyFacts.value: V. Budinský-Krička (excavation 1965, published 1967) and J. Béreš (continuation of the excavation, 1974)

timeline.year: the Late Bronze Age (BD – HA – HB)
timeline.title: The earliest occupation — the Gáva culture
timeline.description: The typologically oldest material at the hillfort belongs to the Gáva culture, which expanded into eastern Slovakia from the south; the first rampart encircling the acropolis testifies to this earliest occupation.

timeline.title: The building of the first acropolis rampart
timeline.description: A rampart with a timber load-bearing construction (charred wood, earth burnt red) typical of the earlier Great Moravian period — the find of a leaf-shaped spearhead can be placed chronologically in the 9th century.

timeline.year: the 10th century, at the latest the early 11th
timeline.title: The main Slavic occupation
timeline.description: V. Budinský-Krička provisionally dated the occupation of the hillfort to this period on the basis of the pottery and iron finds.

timeline.title: A fire-steel from the Morava region
timeline.description: An unusual fire-steel of complex shape attests the contacts of eastern Slovakia with the Morava region; this archaic form of Slavic fire-steel survived in eastern Slovakia into the beginning of the 10th century.

timeline.title: V. Budinský-Krička’s trial excavation
timeline.description: The first archaeological excavation, prompted by J. Macák’s discovery (ramparts, ditches and a dark occupation layer laid bare by the wheels of a tractor).

timeline.title: Publication of the excavation results
timeline.description: V. Budinský-Krička publishes Pokusný výskum na slovanskom hradisku v Šarišských Sokolovciach (A trial excavation at the Slavic hillfort at Šarišské Sokolovce), Nové obzory 9.

timeline.title: J. Béreš continues the excavation
timeline.description: J. Béreš publishes Výsledky doterajšieho výskumu slovanského hradiska v Šarišských Sokolovciach (Results of the excavation to date at the Slavic hillfort at Šarišské Sokolovce), Nové obzory 16.

children.text: The hillfort near Šarišské Sokolovce, discovered by J. Macák, prompted a trial excavation as early as 1965 by virtue of both its position and its fortification by a system of ramparts; it was carried out by the distinguished scholar V. Budinský-Krička. J. Macák’s attention was drawn to this remarkable Slavic monument partly by the folk name of the hill, and partly by the ramparts and ditches of the hillfort and by a dark occupation layer at the places where it had been disturbed and laid bare by the wheels of a tractor.

The hillfort lies 3 km north of Šarišské Sokolovce, in the southern part of the Čergov Mountains. It was built on the highest point of the steep mountainous ridge of Lazíky, which runs between the Bernátske and Bodovské valleys in a north–south direction, on a conical knoll known as the hradová hura. It is accessible from Šarišské Sokolovce through the Bernátske valley, from Bodovce along the ridge of the hill of Lazíky, and from the village of Hradisko from the valley of the Ternianka. The hillfort is well preserved and for the most part protected by dense forest cover. By its position and its fortifications it ranks among the classic examples of a Slavic hillfort in eastern Slovakia. The greatest length of the hillfort is 253 m, the greatest width 125 m.

A small meadow adjoins the north-eastern bend of the hillfort rampart, sloping gently to the west. Roughly in its centre a dark occupation layer was identified on the surface during the trial excavation. In the upper part of the occupation layer relatively few fragments of Hillfort-period pottery were found; from the lower parts of the layer, by contrast, many sherds of this pottery were recovered. The abundant occurrence of sherds at the place of the trial trenches is evidently connected with the proximity of the remains of a large hearth. Besides fragments of vessels, larger or smaller pieces of charcoal were also found in places in the occupation layer, together with isolated fragments of fired clay and two pieces of iron slag. There were no animal bones in it. After the pottery finds, however, the greatest attention is deserved by the iron objects from the lower part of the occupation layer: a fire-steel, a small knife and the torsos of three objects of unknown purpose.

By means of trial trenches V. Budinský-Krička obtained archaeological material from the inner enclosure of the hillfort, and also from outside it on the small meadow that adjoins the rampart on the north-eastern side. The largest quantity of finds consisted of sherd material decorated with wavy lines and incised lines. The small number of iron objects comprised an incomplete fire-steel, an incomplete small knife, a rod-shaped fragment of a mount, a fragment of a hoop from a bucket and a fragment of a small knife. On the basis of the material obtained, V. Budinský-Krička provisionally dated its occupation to the 10th century AD, at the latest to the beginning of the 11th century.

The digging began in the bailey, where trench 1, 40 metres long, cut through the rampart dividing the bailey into two parts, the ditch and the open area, in the direction of the levelling point. In this way the construction of the rampart, a section through the ditch and also the possibility of occupation on the area sloping towards the rampart were investigated. Since no traces of settlement features could be identified in this area, the trench was extended beyond the outer side of the rampart, where there was a terrace, in order to establish whether settlement features adjoined the rampart on this side. Nor did this extension of trench 1 provide any evidence of occupation.

A section through the rampart showed that it had been heaped up from earth and stone. Stone was used above all to reinforce it against the earth slipping into the ditch. Inside the rampart stone occurred in smaller quantities, without any system of laying, that is, merely thrown in loosely. The find inventory from the rampart and the ditch consisted of sherds and animal bones.
Trench 2, 85 metres long, was chosen so that its digging would cut through the circuit rampart with its ditch, the rampart with its ditch encircling the acropolis, and part of the acropolis.

A section through the circuit rampart showed that it too had been heaped up from earth and stone. Stone was used above all to reinforce it against the earth slipping into the ditch. A novelty in the construction system of its heaping up was the identification of traces of charred wood, together with a small band of clay burnt red. This is probably a late survival of the fortification system of the earlier Slavic period. The system by which the rampart was heaped up and the sherd material obtained, an iron arrowhead with backward barbs and the torso of a further arrowhead, give us evidence that it was built by the Slavs evidently in a later period than the first rampart, which encircles the acropolis. In the ditch adjoining the rampart, besides the typical Slavic sherd material obtained during the trial excavation as well as during the digging of trench 1, a sherd with a knob-like boss was found, which proves occupation of the hillfort already in the pre-Slavic period, namely in the Late Bronze Age (
BD – HA – HB
). Apart from sherd material and animal bones, further iron objects were discovered in the ditch: an incomplete arrowhead with backward barbs and an object (
a semi-finished product?
) in the shape of a hammer without a punched hole for a wooden handle.
A section through the first rampart encircling the acropolis showed that it had been built in a different way from the two ramparts already mentioned
(the rampart dividing the bailey into two parts and the circuit rampart

). Its finds also differ from the material obtained in the two last-named ramparts. Its foundation, judging by the surviving remains of charred wood and earth burnt red, was evidently a timber load-bearing construction. This system of heaping up a rampart was typical of the earlier Great Moravian period. The sherd material obtained from it was exclusively of the Late Bronze Age (
BD – HA – HB

). This fact allows the view to be expressed that the first rampart encircling the acropolis testifies to the earliest Slavic occupation of this part. The sherd material and an arrowhead with backward barbs, obtained by digging the trench in the descending part of the terrain towards the ditch adjoining the circuit rampart, together with the sherd material obtained from the ditch belonging to the earliest rampart of the hillfort, are later than the time when this rampart was heaped up.

The digging of the part of trench 2 on the acropolis likewise failed, just as in the cases of trench 1 mentioned above, to yield any traces of settlement features. This circumstance led to trench 3 being laid out and dug to a length of 10 metres on a level clearing in a south-easterly direction from the levelling point. During its digging, beneath the humic layer of the terrain, an occupation pit containing sherd material was discovered. Immediately beside it was an area burnt red, together with charred remains of wood, indicating part of the floor of a hut. Because it exceeded the width of the trench, part of trench 4 had to be laid out and dug in order to capture it in full. In its immediate vicinity, stones laid flat and transversely in the shape of an irregular rectangle were found, which probably formed a single complex with the floor. The author provisionally regards it as the stone casing of an oven (
a fireplace?
). This assumption and its connection with part of the floor of the hut will be verified by the continuation of the excavation.

In the second bailey, trenches 5 and 6, 45 metres long, were laid out and dug intermittently. They were intended to establish the situation on the open space of the meadow within the enclosure of the hillfort. In both trenches, besides sherd material, fragments of daub and iron slag were found. In neither of them were traces of settlement features, or possibly of a smithy’s forge, recorded, although the fragments of daub and pieces of iron slag are evidence of them. This is probably connected with the fact that the features within the enclosure of the hillfort were of a ground-level character, or only slightly sunk into the ground, made of wood and wattle and plastered with daub. After the hillfort ceased to function, they too were destroyed in the course of the centuries without traces being preserved (
the washing away of the occupation layer

Trench 7, 20 metres long, was laid out on the forest track leading through the enclosure of the hillfort up to the acropolis, so that it cut across the rampart with its ditch on the slope of the acropolis and of the first bailey. Its digging was to establish the construction of the rampart and its chronological relationship to the first rampart, which encircles the acropolis, and to the other ramparts of the hillfort. In this trench traces of a timber construction of the rampart were again identified
(charred wood)
, together with sherd material of the Late Bronze Age and of the Slavic period, and also a well-preserved iron leaf-shaped spearhead
(at a depth of 75 cm

). The surviving remains of charred wood from the construction of the rampart, the sherds of the Late Bronze Age, an isolated Slavic sherd and the iron leaf-shaped spearhead allow the view to be expressed that it was built by the population living on the acropolis still before the 10th century, in order to prevent easy access to the acropolis from the north-western side. A closer chronological placing of the individual ramparts in which traces of a timber construction were found will certainly be provided by analyses of the remains of charred wood.

Analysis of the find inventory I. Pottery The pottery material obtained by the excavation of the hillfort at Šarišské Sokolovce to date forms the most numerous component of the find inventory. It consists of numerous diagnostic fragments, from which complete vessels could not be reconstructed. Because these are finds obtained from sections through the ramparts and ditches as well as from trenches outside them, where fragments of typologically older vessels were mixed with fragments of pottery of a later character, and not from closed settlement features, we proceed from this aspect also in classifying the material, especially the Slavic material.
a)
Typologically the oldest material that has been found at the hillfort in the excavations to date is material from the earlier part of the Late Bronze Age (
BD – HA – HB
), belonging for the present in eastern Slovakia to the Gáva culture, which expanded here from the south.

Particularly noteworthy is the coarser sherd material of a pale brown colour with a smooth coating on the surface, which probably comes from larger pot-shaped vessels. It was mostly undecorated. Only occasionally did decoration in the form of a simple oval boss occur on it. Isolated pottery remains also occurred representing types of vessel rim and, in one case, part of a base. A thinner sherd of a light brown colour with a rim slightly rounded inwards evidently comes from a bowl. Two rim sherds, of which one has a coarser rounded rim and the other a broader everted rim, came from pot-shaped vessels. The sherd from the base of a vessel had a porous surface and a coarsely formed uneven base. The author regards an isolated coarser sherd of a dark grey colour as a representative of perhaps the local Late Piliny population.
b)

In classifying the Slavic pottery material obtained so far from the hillfort, it appears that its smaller part is still closely related to Middle Hillfort-period pottery. The greater part, however, belongs to later Hillfort-period pottery.

The sherds of the earlier Slavic pottery come from thin-walled and thick-walled pots of brown, brownish-grey and dark grey colour, with a rough surface, well fired, made of clay with an admixture of limestone, sand and mica. The necks of the vessels, judging by some rim sherds, were not widely open and were cut vertically or obliquely at the rim. On some fragments the beginnings of a profiling of the vessel rim are already discernible. The ornament on the sherds consists of multiple wavy lines and of bands of horizontal lines.

Perhaps also belonging to the earlier group of finds from Šarišské Sokolovce is a fragment from the base of a brownish-grey vessel with a faintly visible part of a probably rectangular relief mark. It is the second different type of occurrence of a relief mark obtained in the excavation of the hillfort to date. In the first case it was part of a relief mark in the shape of a square.
To the earlier Slavic pottery we assign a sherd decorated with oblique circumferential bands made with impressions of a comb-like tool.

According to insights from the Morava region and other areas, it is quite possible that fragments of vessels decorated with coarsely and individually incised wavy lines and horizontal lines also belong to the earlier pottery from the hillfort, and that conversely some fragments of an archaic character may already be connected with the later Slavic phase at the hillfort.

The largest quantity of sherds obtained by the excavation of the hillfort to date belongs to advanced Hillfort-period pottery. These are fragments of vessels already with more pronounced features of rim profiling, or with a cornice-like rim, in some cases already very close to medieval pottery. As regards decoration, the sherds that belong here are mainly those from vessels decorated on and below the neck with a coarse incised wavy line or wavy lines, and on the body with horizontal lines, sometimes sparse, at other times denser or covering the whole surface quite continuously. The continuous grooving of the body of the vessels sometimes created a markedly furrowed surface. With this form of decoration these vessels already came considerably close to medieval pottery.

The vessels were probably already made on a more rapidly turned wheel, as is indicated above all by the fine horizontal strokes or grooves in the coating of the sherds. The clay, as well as the colour of the pottery fragments, does not differ from the typologically earlier pottery. Some rim sherds bear traces on the inner side of working with a toothed implement. On the basis of the decoration of the pottery it may be judged that the decoration was incised into the coating of the vessels with a blunt rod, exceptionally also with a comb-like tool.

That pottery at the hillfort at Šarišské Sokolovce was an important commodity in the later period as well, and that it was used to the maximum, is shown by a fragment of a vessel pierced in order to strengthen a cracked part.
In several cases remains of a black organic substance have survived on the inner side of the walls of the sherds (
perhaps traces of food)

. Chemical analysis would probably make it possible to determine what kind of food is involved, and on this basis one could also gain a partial glimpse into the “kitchen” of our Slavic ancestors who lived at the hillfort at Šarišské Sokolovce.

II. Iron objects Of the finds of this kind obtained in the outer enclosure of the hillfort, undoubtedly the most remarkable and most important is the torso of a fire-steel of complex shape with triply bent arms; it is 8.6 cm long and 3.6 cm wide. The fire-steel is of a completely different type from the grave finds of iron fire-steels of the Slav–Avar and Old Hungarian periods in eastern Slovakia known hitherto.

The fire-steel from Šarišské Sokolovce is thus a further interesting and weighty monument drawing attention to the contacts of eastern Slovakia in the hillfort period with the Morava region. If, on the basis of the pottery finds from the hillfort, it can be dated as late as the post-Great Moravian period, then it is remarkable that this archaic form of Slavic fire-steel survived precisely in eastern Slovakia into the beginning of the 10th century.

The small knife has a broken-off tip, and only an insignificant part of the tang of its handle has survived. The back of the blade is slightly bent and is separated from the tang by an oblique step. The cutting edge of the knife runs approximately in a straight line parallel to the lower edge of the handle. The torso is 9 cm long and 1.8 cm wide. It is a small knife of Hillfort-period form that cannot be dated more closely, belonging rather to the Middle Hillfort period.
The flat rod-shaped iron object in the shape of a long trapezium is a fragment of a mount or of a tool of unknown purpose; it is 8.8 cm long and at most 2.1 cm wide.
The other two iron objects are atypical; one of them is as it were a fragment of a hoop from a bucket (
length 3.7 cm)
, the other, with an arched cutting edge, is perhaps a fragment of a knife (
length 4.3 cm and max. width 2.1 cm

Finds of this kind in the inner enclosure formed only an insignificant number in comparison with the quantity of pottery obtained. Their small typological range consisted of three arrowheads with backward barbs ending in a socket, the torso of an iron arrowhead, a leaf-shaped spearhead with a shorter round socket, and an iron object (
a semi-finished product?
) in the shape of a hammer, on which the punched hole for a wooden handle is missing.

Iron arrowheads with backward barbs ending in a socket were suitable both for hunting and for fighting, because they caused a lacerated wound and thus accelerated bleeding to death. Because these were weapons that could usually be used only once, no complicated manufacturing process was employed in their production. This type of arrowhead has been known since the Late La Tène period, surviving through the Roman period and the hillfort period into the Middle Ages.
The find of a leaf-shaped spearhead with a shorter, conically widening socket and a broader, thickened blade can be placed chronologically in the 9th century.
The iron object, (
a semi-finished product?

) judging by its shape, was originally meant to be a hammer. Because it is, however, without a punched hole for a wooden handle, the author regards it as a semi-finished product which, judging by the distinct impacts on the butt as well as by the uneven end of the narrowed part, was probably used as a punch.

Apart from the iron components of armament and a working tool, pieces of iron slag were also found during the excavation of the hillfort, in the second bailey. These finds, together with similar ones obtained by the trial excavation outside the enclosure of the hillfort on the small meadow immediately adjoining it, are evidence of the existence of smithing both within the enclosure of the hillfort and in the part belonging to it beyond the fortification.

III. Iron slag R. Pleiner of the Institute of Archaeology of the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences in Prague expressed the view that this is waste from a smithy. These are essentially iron oxides worked at a temperature of over 1,200 °C. They testify to the existence of smithing at the hillfort, not to the metallurgical processing of iron.

IV. Charcoal Samples of charcoal from the occupation layer uncovered on the platform outside the rampart of the hillfort were identified by E. Krippel of the Dionýz Štúr Institute of Geology in Bratislava in two cases as coming from elm (
Ulmus
) and in one case as coming from beech (
Fagus
). This identification is noteworthy above all because today hornbeam predominates in the forest cover at the hillfort and in its surroundings.
The origin of the remains of the black, charred, structureless organic substance from the walls of some vessels
(most likely traces of food)
could, according to E. Krippel, perhaps be determined by chemical means.
